difficultyReason: The argument rests on a hidden methodological assumption: that the control group in a longitudinal study is comparable to the treatment group. The correct weakener attacks this buried comparability premise rather than either named variable. Distractors include a strengthener, an adjacent-premise attacker, an out-of-scope comparison, and a narrowly scoped fact.
stimulus: A pharmaceutical researcher concluded that a new antidepressant, Velanol, reduces the frequency of depressive episodes. The researcher based this on a five-year study in which patients who took Velanol reported 40 percent fewer depressive episodes per year than patients who received no medication. The researcher controlled for age, sex, and baseline depression severity at enrollment.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the researcher's conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Patients who received no medication in the study were significantly more likely to have refused prior antidepressant treatment, suggesting higher baseline resistance to standard interventions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Velanol was well tolerated by most participants, with fewer than 8 percent reporting adverse side effects serious enough to discontinue use.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Several other antidepressants on the market also reduce the frequency of depressive episodes in clinical trials.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The five-year study period coincided with an era of unusually low economic stress, which is known to correlate with reduced depression rates generally.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Patients who enrolled in the study were screened for co-occurring anxiety disorders before being assigned to either group.

explanations.correct: The researcher controls for age, sex, and baseline depression severity, but not for treatment history. If unmedicated patients were systematically more treatment-resistant, the groups are not truly comparable, and the 40-percent gap may reflect a selection difference rather than Velanol's effect. This attacks the hidden assumption of group comparability that the study's causal conclusion depends on.
explanations.A: Correct. Introduces a confounding selection difference (treatment resistance) not accounted for in the controls, undermining the causal inference.
explanations.B: Irrelevant to efficacy. High tolerability slightly bolsters the case for Velanol as a practical treatment option but does not bear on the premise-to-conclusion move. Opposite-direction trap.
explanations.C: Shift-in-subject trap. Whether other drugs work tells us nothing about whether Velanol specifically caused the observed reduction; leaves the conclusion standing.
explanations.D: This is a plausible confounder (economic climate → depression rates), but it is symmetric — it would lower episode rates in both groups equally — so it cannot explain the 40-percent difference between groups. Too narrow to undermine the conclusion.
explanations.E: Describes a screening procedure that, if anything, strengthens the methodological rigor of the study. Strengthener trap.

difficultyReason: Multi-step causal chain (deforestation → soil erosion → river sedimentation → fish decline). The correct weakener attacks the B→C link in a way that leaves A→B intact, requiring the student to identify which link carries the conclusion. Distractors attack A→B or offer irrelevant environmental facts.
stimulus: A regional environmental agency argued that logging operations in the upper watershed have caused the steep decline in native fish populations observed over the past decade. The agency cited data showing that deforestation sharply increased soil erosion rates in the watershed, and that elevated soil erosion consistently leads to river sedimentation. Since sedimentation is known to destroy fish spawning beds, the logging must be responsible for the fish decline.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The logging companies operating in the watershed replanted approximately 60 percent of cleared areas within three years of harvesting.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Sediment levels in the affected rivers have not risen measurably over the past decade, despite increased erosion rates in the upper watershed.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Native fish populations in unlogged watersheds in the same region have also declined over the same period.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Soil erosion in the upper watershed was already elevated before logging operations began, due to periodic drought cycles.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Researchers have documented that sedimentation harms fish spawning in rivers worldwide, not only in this region.

explanations.correct: The argument's conclusion depends on the chain: deforestation → erosion → sedimentation → fish decline. Choice B severs the erosion-to-sedimentation link by showing that despite higher erosion rates, river sediment levels have not actually risen. Without elevated sedimentation, the spawning-bed destruction mechanism collapses, and so does the case for blaming logging.
explanations.A: Attacks the extent of deforestation (A→B link) but only partially — 40 percent of cleared areas were not replanted. Does not sever any single link cleanly enough to undermine the conclusion significantly.
explanations.B: Correct. Severs the critical erosion→sedimentation link, dismantling the causal mechanism the argument relies on.
explanations.C: Alternative-explanation trap, but weaker than B: fish declines elsewhere suggest a region-wide factor, but the agency's argument is specifically about the mechanism (sedimentation), not mere correlation. This choice raises doubt about correlation without attacking the stated mechanism.
explanations.D: Pre-existing erosion weakens the implied uniqueness of logging as an erosion source but does not address whether logging contributed additionally or whether sedimentation actually occurred. Too narrow.
explanations.E: Strengthens by confirming the sedimentation-to-fish-decline link is well-established. Opposite-direction trap.

difficultyReason: An economics argument predicting a future outcome rests on an analogy to a prior episode. The hidden assumption is that the analogy holds. The correct weakener identifies a disanalogy that undermines the prediction. Distractors include a strengthener, an irrelevant historical fact, and one answer that weakens the analogy's premise rather than the conclusion.
stimulus: An economic analyst argued that the government's planned 15-percent tariff on imported steel will reduce domestic steel prices within two years. The analyst cited the tariff imposed on imported aluminum in 2012, after which domestic aluminum prices fell by 12 percent within 18 months as domestic producers, now shielded from foreign competition, invested in efficiency-enhancing technology and passed savings on to buyers.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The domestic steel industry is currently operating at near full capacity, leaving producers little room to invest in additional efficiency improvements.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The 2012 aluminum tariff was slightly lower, at 13 percent, than the steel tariff being proposed today.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Several economists who opposed the 2012 aluminum tariff have since revised their assessments in light of the price data.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Domestic steel producers lobbied heavily for the proposed tariff, suggesting they anticipate increased profitability.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Consumer demand for steel has remained stable over the past five years, even as global steel production increased.

explanations.correct: The analyst's prediction depends on the same mechanism that lowered aluminum prices: protected domestic producers invest in efficiency technology and pass savings to buyers. If the steel industry is already at full capacity, that mechanism cannot operate — there is no room for efficiency investment — so the analogical prediction fails. This is a precise disanalogy attacking the causal mechanism, not just a surface difference.
explanations.A: Correct. Undercuts the efficiency-investment mechanism that drove price reduction in the aluminum case, breaking the analogy at its load-bearing assumption.
explanations.B: The 2-percentage-point difference in tariff levels is immaterial to whether the mechanism operates; it does not expose a meaningful disanalogy. Accurate-but-irrelevant trap.
explanations.C: Strengthens by adding credibility to the aluminum-tariff precedent. Opposite-direction trap.
explanations.D: If anything, strengthens the idea that producers see profit potential, which could include efficiency investment. Opposite-direction trap.
explanations.E: Stable demand establishes a baseline but does not address whether producers will invest in efficiency; irrelevant to the analogical mechanism.

difficultyReason: A policy argument uses a generalization from a pilot program to a national rollout. The correct weakener shows the pilot sample is non-representative in a way that is not obvious from the stimulus. Distractors include a near-miss that attacks program design rather than representativeness, a strengthener, and an out-of-scope policy comparison.
stimulus: A policy adviser urged the federal government to mandate financial literacy courses in all public high schools nationwide. As evidence, the adviser cited a three-year pilot program in forty rural school districts, in which graduating students who completed the course were 30 percent more likely than non-participants to maintain a positive savings balance one year after graduation. The adviser concluded that a nationwide mandate would produce similarly significant improvements in young adults' financial outcomes.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The forty rural districts selected for the pilot were chosen in part because their school boards had already expressed strong support for financial literacy education, making their students and teachers unusually predisposed to engagement with the curriculum.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The financial literacy curriculum used in the pilot program took three years to develop and required substantial teacher training before implementation.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Some students who completed the financial literacy course reported that the material was too advanced for their grade level.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Several other countries that have adopted mandatory financial literacy requirements in secondary schools have reported positive outcomes for young adults.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Students in the pilot program who did not take the course had lower average household incomes than those who did.

explanations.correct: The adviser's generalization from pilot to nationwide mandate assumes the pilot sample is representative. Choice A reveals the pilot districts were self-selected for unusual institutional buy-in, making the results ungeneralizable — a mandatory rollout to all districts, including resistant ones, would not replicate the conditions that produced the 30-percent gain. This attacks the hidden representativeness assumption.
explanations.A: Correct. Exposes a critical selection bias: the pilot districts were predisposed to success, so the result cannot be generalized to all schools nationwide.
explanations.B: Attacks implementation feasibility, not the logical move from pilot results to national prediction. A difficult rollout might slow adoption but doesn't undermine the underlying causal relationship the adviser asserts. Too narrow.
explanations.C: Identifies a curriculum design issue but doesn't show the improvement outcome is wrong — students may have found it challenging yet still benefited. Irrelevant to the conclusion's scope.
explanations.D: Strengthens by providing corroborating international evidence. Opposite-direction trap.
explanations.E: This actually weakens the comparison within the pilot (the control group was poorer), but it attacks the internal validity of the pilot itself rather than the generalizability to the national level. Because the conclusion is about national rollout efficacy, this is a too-narrow trap — it raises doubt about the pilot's own numbers but leaves the generalization assumption untouched.

difficultyReason: A legal argument relies on an unstated principle — that legislative silence implies permission. The correct weakener introduces evidence that undermines this interpretive principle in a way that requires understanding the implicit move from 'statute does not mention X' to 'X is therefore allowed.' Distractors include a choice that strengthens the interpretation and one that shifts to an adjacent legal question.
stimulus: A defense attorney argued that her client's use of automated bidding software during an online auction did not violate the auction platform's terms of service. The attorney pointed out that the terms of service explicitly prohibit 'deceptive practices' and 'manual bid manipulation' but make no mention of automated software. Since the terms do not prohibit automated bidding, the client's conduct must be considered permissible under the agreement.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the attorney's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The platform's terms of service were drafted before automated bidding software was widely available, and the drafters have since publicly stated that all non-human bidding methods were intended to fall within the prohibition on bid manipulation.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Courts in the jurisdiction have consistently held that online auction terms of service are enforceable contracts.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The client used the automated software openly and did not attempt to conceal its use from the platform.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Other auction platforms operating in the same market have explicitly banned automated bidding in their terms of service.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The platform's terms of service prohibit 'deceptive practices,' a category that some courts have interpreted broadly.

explanations.correct: The attorney's argument rests on legislative/contractual silence implying permission: because automated bidding is not explicitly named, it is allowed. Choice A demolishes this by showing the silence was a drafting gap, not intentional permission — the drafters publicly stated automated bidding was meant to fall under the 'bid manipulation' prohibition. This defeats the 'not mentioned = permitted' interpretive principle that the argument depends on.
explanations.A: Correct. Shows the silence was inadvertent, not permissive, directly undermining the inference from omission to authorization.
explanations.B: Strengthens by confirming the terms are legally binding — if anything, this makes the prohibition on 'bid manipulation' more potent. Opposite-direction trap.
explanations.C: The attorney's argument is about the terms' text, not intent to deceive; openness of use is legally irrelevant to whether the terms were violated. Accurate-but-irrelevant trap.
explanations.D: Shift-in-subject trap. What competitors prohibit tells us nothing about what this platform's silence means; other platforms' rules don't interpret this contract.
explanations.E: Weakens the attorney's position only obliquely — the conclusion is about automated bidding, not 'deceptive practices.' This answer would weaken only if automated bidding were already classified as deceptive, which hasn't been established. Too narrow / shift in subject.

difficultyReason: A technology argument draws a causal conclusion from a before-and-after productivity metric without ruling out a specific type of confound: a parallel organizational change. The correct weakener introduces that confound. Distractors include a strengthener disguised as a process detail, an irrelevant industry comparison, and a choice that attacks the metric's validity without touching the conclusion.
stimulus: A management consultant reported that after a mid-sized software firm adopted an AI-assisted code-review tool, the average time developers spent fixing bugs dropped by 35 percent over the following year. The consultant concluded that the AI tool was responsible for the improvement in developer productivity.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The AI code-review tool was developed by a third-party vendor with extensive experience in software quality assurance.

choices.label: B
choices.text: During the same year, the firm restructured its engineering teams, reducing team sizes and pairing senior developers with junior ones — a configuration independently shown to reduce debugging time by up to 40 percent.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Developers at the firm reported high satisfaction with the AI tool in anonymous surveys conducted six months after its adoption.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Several competing software firms adopted similar AI code-review tools in the same period without reporting comparable productivity gains.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Time spent fixing bugs is only one component of total developer productivity, which also includes time spent on new feature development and documentation.

explanations.correct: The consultant's conclusion is causal: the AI tool caused the 35-percent drop in debugging time. Choice B introduces a simultaneous organizational change — team restructuring with senior-junior pairings — that is independently documented to reduce debugging time by a comparable or greater magnitude. This alternative explanation directly undermines the attribution of the improvement to the AI tool.
explanations.A: Vendor experience is irrelevant to whether the tool caused the improvement; it speaks to product quality, not causation. Accurate-but-irrelevant trap.
explanations.B: Correct. Classic alternative-explanation weakener: a parallel intervention with known, documented efficacy that could account for the observed improvement.
explanations.C: Strengthens the inference by suggesting developers found the tool valuable, implying use was substantive. Opposite-direction trap.
explanations.D: This might seem to weaken, but competitor results are a shift-in-subject trap — the argument is about this specific firm's results, and different firms' implementations may vary in fidelity or context.
explanations.E: Attacks the adequacy of the productivity metric but does not challenge the causal claim that the AI tool caused the observed reduction in the metric that was measured. Premise-attacker-without-touching-conclusion trap.

difficultyReason: An ethics argument from a universal moral principle to a specific policy conclusion. The hidden assumption is that the principle applies to the class of cases in question. The correct weakener shows a relevant difference that exempts the case from the principle's scope — requiring students to distinguish 'weakens the principle' from 'weakens the application of the principle to this case.'
stimulus: An ethicist argued that hospitals should never disclose a patient's medical information to law enforcement without explicit patient consent. The ethicist's reasoning was that respect for personal autonomy requires that individuals retain control over sensitive personal information, and medical information is among the most sensitive categories of personal data.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Patient autonomy is widely recognized as a foundational principle in biomedical ethics.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Law enforcement agencies sometimes request medical information without sufficient legal justification.

choices.label: C
choices.text: When a patient poses a credible, specific threat of serious violence to an identifiable third party, the patient's autonomy interest is outweighed by the potential victim's right to protection — a conclusion the ethicist has endorsed in other contexts.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Many jurisdictions already have statutory frameworks that require court orders before hospitals must comply with law enforcement requests for medical records.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Medical information is defined differently under privacy law in different countries, making a universal standard difficult to implement.

explanations.correct: The ethicist's argument is that autonomy always requires patient consent before disclosure. Choice C introduces a category the ethicist has already acknowledged as an exception — credible, specific threats of violence — and applies it to this context. This shows the 'never disclose without consent' conclusion is too absolute because the ethicist's own stated values permit exceptions that would allow disclosure. This undermines the universal claim by showing a class of cases the principle, by the ethicist's own lights, does not cover.
explanations.A: Strengthens by affirming the foundational premise (patient autonomy matters). Opposite-direction trap.
explanations.B: Attacks the behavior of law enforcement, not the logical move from the autonomy principle to the 'never disclose' conclusion. Even if true, unjustified requests could be screened without a blanket prohibition. Shift-in-subject trap.
explanations.C: Correct. Shows the ethicist's own commitment to victim-protection rights in analogous cases undermines the absolute 'never' in the conclusion — the principle does not apply uniformly to all disclosure situations.
explanations.D: Addresses practical implementation and existing law, not the normative argument. Accurate-but-irrelevant trap.
explanations.E: International variation in legal definitions is irrelevant to the normative ethical argument, which does not depend on legal uniformity. Out-of-scope trap.

difficultyReason: A historical argument uses a single episode to support a broad causal generalization. The correct weakener shows the episode is anomalous in a way that invalidates the generalization, but this requires recognizing the specific historical feature that made the episode unique. Distractors include a strengthener that cites a parallel episode and a too-narrow choice that addresses only one dimension of the anomaly.
stimulus: A historian argued that economic depressions are the primary cause of democratic backsliding. The historian pointed to the collapse of the Weimar Republic in Germany during the early 1930s: a devastating economic depression coincided with the rise of authoritarianism, and the historian claimed this pattern demonstrates that economic hardship reliably produces conditions favorable to authoritarian takeover.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Weimar Republic was also subject to specific structural weaknesses — including a fragmented party system, provisions enabling emergency rule, and the political legacies of World War I — that made it uniquely susceptible to authoritarian capture independent of economic conditions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Several democracies experienced severe economic depressions during the twentieth century without undergoing democratic backsliding.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Authoritarianism tends to produce economic decline, suggesting the causal relationship between economics and political systems may run in the opposite direction.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Great Depression of the 1930s affected many countries simultaneously, producing varied political outcomes across different national contexts.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Historians disagree about the relative weight of economic versus political causes in the fall of the Weimar Republic.

explanations.correct: The historian's argument is a generalization: economic depressions reliably cause democratic backsliding. Choice B directly refutes this generalization by citing counterexamples — democracies that survived severe economic depressions without backsliding. These counterexamples show the claimed reliable causal relationship does not hold universally, undermining the move from the Weimar case to the broader conclusion.
explanations.A: This identifies confounds in the Weimar case, which calls into question whether the depression — rather than structural factors — was the cause in that specific episode. However, the argument's conclusion is a general causal claim about economic depressions and democratic backsliding broadly, not just about Weimar. Choice A weakens the premise (the Weimar example) but not the broader conclusion as directly as B does. Too-narrow trap.
explanations.B: Correct. Provides direct counterexamples to the general causal claim, the most powerful form of weakening a causal generalization.
explanations.C: Reversed-causation trap. While this introduces an alternative causal direction, it does not address the specific claim that depressions cause backsliding — it would need to show the Weimar sequence ran in reverse to directly undermine the argument.
explanations.D: Similar to A — varied outcomes during the Great Depression suggest other factors matter, but this is less precise and direct than B's explicit counterexamples. Weaker version of B.
explanations.E: Scholarly disagreement about causes is meta-evidence about the difficulty of the question, not evidence about the causal relationship itself. Accurate-but-irrelevant trap.

difficultyReason: A linguistics argument about language change uses corpus frequency data to infer a causal mechanism (prescriptive instruction causing decline of a grammatical form). The correct weakener shows the frequency data could reflect a different methodological artifact rather than real-world language change. Distractors include a strengthener, a shift to a different language feature, and a choice that attacks a side premise without touching the conclusion.
stimulus: A linguist argued that prescriptive grammar instruction in schools is causing the decline of the subjunctive mood in English. The linguist cited corpus data showing that subjunctive constructions appeared 40 percent less frequently in written texts produced after 1990 than in texts from the 1960s. Since grammar instruction intensified in the 1970s and 1980s, the linguist concluded that teaching prescriptive rules paradoxically suppresses students' awareness of the subjunctive, leading to its disuse.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most calls into question the linguist's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The corpus used to measure post-1990 written texts drew primarily from online forums and informal digital communication, whereas the 1960s corpus consisted almost entirely of formal published prose.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Some linguists argue that the subjunctive mood is being replaced by modal auxiliaries such as 'might' and 'should,' rather than simply disappearing from English.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Grammar instruction in many school districts became less prescriptive after 2000, yet subjunctive use has not recovered in recent corpus analyses.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Prescriptive grammar instruction in the 1970s focused primarily on punctuation and sentence structure rather than on mood distinctions.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Several European languages with more extensive subjunctive systems have also experienced declining subjunctive use over the same period.

explanations.correct: The linguist's argument depends on the corpus frequency drop as evidence of real-world language change caused by grammar instruction. Choice A exposes a methodological artifact: the post-1990 corpus overrepresents informal digital communication (where subjunctive use is naturally lower) while the 1960s corpus captured formal prose (where it is naturally higher). The frequency difference may reflect a genre shift in corpus composition rather than any change in language behavior driven by instruction. This undermines the data's reliability as evidence of the claimed trend.
explanations.A: Correct. Identifies a corpus composition artifact that could entirely explain the frequency difference, making the data unreliable as evidence of the claimed language change.
explanations.B: Addresses how the subjunctive may be functionally replaced, which if anything supports a real decline — it doesn't challenge the data or the causal claim about instruction. Partially-relevant but insufficient trap.
explanations.C: This actually strengthens the argument by suggesting the decline persists even when the proposed cause weakened — but it is a complex distractor because it could also suggest instruction wasn't the cause. On balance, the lack of recovery after instruction eased could suggest the decline is real and entrenched, slightly supporting the claim. Opposite-direction or ambiguous trap.
explanations.D: Weakens the premise that grammar instruction in the 1970s focused on mood distinctions — attacking the 'instruction intensified' premise. But even if instruction didn't target mood specifically, another kind of prescriptivism could have the suppressive effect. This is a too-narrow attack on one premise that leaves the broader causal conclusion standing through other routes.
explanations.E: Parallel trends in other languages suggest the change may be a broader typological shift, not caused by English-specific school instruction. This is a legitimate weakener but less precise than A, which attacks the data quality itself rather than providing an alternative explanation at the macro level. Second-best distractor.

difficultyReason: An arts/cultural policy argument predicts that public arts funding cuts will cause a decline in domestic artistic output, relying on an implicit assumption about the relationship between funding and production. The correct weakener attacks this assumption by showing a structural difference that severs the link, and requires distinguishing it from a choice that strengthens the argument by confirming the funding-output relationship holds elsewhere.
stimulus: A cultural policy advocate argued that the proposed 25-percent cut to the National Arts Endowment's grants program will lead to a significant decline in the production of original domestic artworks over the next five years. The advocate noted that endowment grants currently provide the primary income for nearly 60 percent of working artists in the country, and that without income, artists cannot afford to produce work.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Several major private foundations have announced plans to increase arts grants by an amount that would offset the proposed endowment cuts, specifically targeting artists who currently rely on endowment funding.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The endowment's grants program has historically supported artists working in traditional media more heavily than those working in digital or emerging art forms.

choices.label: C
choices.text: In countries where public arts funding was reduced sharply, artistic output declined within a similar timeframe.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Many artists who receive endowment grants supplement their income with teaching, commissions, or commercial work.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The National Arts Endowment administers a separate program for arts education that is not subject to the proposed cut.

explanations.correct: The advocate's argument assumes that the funding cut will deprive artists of income and thereby reduce production. Choice A directly severs this link: if private foundations will compensate with offsetting grants specifically targeting affected artists, the income loss does not occur, and the predicted production decline has no mechanism. This is a classic 'compensating factor' weakener that attacks the crucial premise that artists will lack income.
explanations.A: Correct. Introduces a compensating mechanism that prevents the predicted causal sequence from unfolding — no income loss means the production decline prediction fails.
explanations.B: Identifies a distributional feature of current grants (favoring traditional media) that is irrelevant to whether a funding cut reduces total output. Accurate-but-irrelevant trap.
explanations.C: Strengthens by providing comparative evidence that the predicted pattern (funding cut → output decline) has occurred elsewhere. Opposite-direction trap.
explanations.D: Partially weakens by suggesting some artists have income sources beyond endowment grants, but the advocate's claim was about the 60 percent who rely on grants as their primary income — supplemental income from teaching doesn't necessarily compensate for a 25-percent cut to primary income. Too-narrow trap; doesn't fully sever the link.
explanations.E: The separate arts education program is outside the scope of the argument, which concerns artistic production, not arts education. Shift-in-subject trap.
